strengths: The paper addresses a relevant NLP problem: forecasting pretraining loss early enough to inform training decisions. Modeling loss by token position provides a useful empirical perspective on context-dependent learning.

The experimental coverage is substantial, spanning LLaMA-style models from 9.8M to 6.7B parameters, ID and OOD evaluation, and additional GPT-NeoX and MoE architectures. Figures 3 and 5 evaluate future-loss prediction, beyond retrospective curve fitting, and show consistent improvements over the three reported baselines.

The data-mixture application includes completed training runs: Table 4 reports lower final perplexity in all four comparisons, and Table 3 reports improvements on 12 of 14 model–benchmark combinations. Explicit equations, architecture tables, package versions, and pseudocode provide useful implementation guidance.
weaknesses: The central comparison does not isolate the contribution of token-position modeling. The proposed predictor incorporates a flexible piecewise double-log/cosine function and the known training horizon, whereas the baselines use simpler global functions without equivalent schedule information. After a0 and a1 are frozen, Equation 10 reduces to a constant plus a2(N). A direct aggregate-loss predictor using the same piecewise form and schedule information is therefore an essential missing control.

Important reproducibility details remain unspecified: nonlinear fitting initialization and constraints, the outlier-removal threshold, evaluation frequency, and the actual searched and selected mixture weights. No implementation or loss-trace release is linked. Algorithm 1, lines 29–30, also applies calibration when Npred <= Nsep, contradicting Section 2.4, which requires observations after the separation point. These gaps prevent confident reproduction of the reported forecasting results.

The practical selection evidence is promising but insufficiently characterized. Selection occurs after 10B of 400B tokens, or 2.5% of training, while the forecasting evaluation starts at 10%. Candidate-wise predicted versus realized losses and ranking accuracy are not reported. The final perplexity improvements are only 0.05–0.15, without uncertainty across independent runs; averaging the last five checkpoints does not establish robustness to training randomness. The total candidate-search cost is also unspecified.

The theoretical interpretation exceeds what is established. Equation 17 follows directly from manually freezing a0 and a1 in Equation 8; Figure 11 provides empirical support for approximately uniform loss decreases, but this does not establish that positional reweighting is unnecessary. Testing three suppression heuristics supports only a limited conclusion. Appendix C also rejects exponential decay after imposing a zero offset, although an exponential with a positive offset satisfies the proposed nonzero-asymptote requirement.

Generality and novelty need more precise qualification. All training uses English Pile data and cosine schedules; the additional architectures primarily demonstrate retrospective fits rather than forecasting generalization. Kaplan et al. (2020) already investigate step-dependent learning curves, making the blanket claim that temporal loss modeling is unexplored too strong. The empirical results make a Findings contribution plausible, but the missing matched controls and reproducibility details leave the recommendation borderline.
